title: Why Are So Many Disembodied Feet Washing Ashore In British Columbia?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the series of disembodied feet found washing ashore in British Columbia and Washington State between 2007 and 2016, starting with a shoe-and-foot discovery on Jedediah Island in August 2007. They walk through the identified cases (mostly people who died by suicide or accidents near water), how bodies sink, bloat, and disarticulate underwater, why athletic shoes keep feet afloat and intact, a 2016 Simon Fraser University pig-carcass sinking study, a King County medical examiner's study of underwater decomposition, British Columbia's high rate of missing persons, and the frequency illusion as a possible explanation for the perceived clustering. The episode ends with a listener Internet Roundup segment about a bumpy Delta flight and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter about feet
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about where feet belong, airplane seat-back and shoe-removal etiquette, and then introduce the topic of feet found on beaches.

segments.title: First foot on Jedediah Island and second foot on Gabriola Island
segments.summary: In August 2007 a twelve-year-old girl found a foot in a Campus brand shoe on Jedediah Island in British Columbia. Police and coroner investigated, and DNA found no match. Six days later a right foot in a Reebok shoe turned up on Gabriola Island, and Corporal Gary Cox commented on the odds.

segments.title: Media attention and British Columbia missing persons
segments.summary: Media coverage began as the feet piled up, coinciding with the Robert Pickton trial. The hosts discuss the theory of serial killers, and a Christopher Solomon observation that British Columbia has a higher rate of unsolved missing persons than Kentucky.

segments.title: Tsunami theory and other explanations
segments.summary: Some suggested the feet came from tsunami victims of the 2004 Indian Ocean disaster, and the hosts discuss this alongside the film The Impossible. Others pointed to people who vanish in the Salish Sea, such as plane crashes.

segments.title: Third through seventh feet and identifications
segments.summary: A woman's New Balance-type shoe foot was found on Kirkland Island, with five feet from four people within ten months. A Nike foot and a sixth foot in Washington followed. The seventh was the woman's other foot. Identified cases were tied to suicides by depression, a jump from a bridge, and an accident after a boat capsized.
topics: suicide and accidental deaths near water

segments.title: How bodies sink, bloat and float underwater
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck explain that drowned bodies usually sink quickly, that saltwater and fat affect buoyancy, that cold water and pressure slow decomposition, and that gases from bacteria cause bloating and eventual rising unless the body is trapped or ruptures. They recount a case of cars submerged in Fosse Lake, Oklahoma.

segments.title: Pig carcass study, disarticulation, and athletic shoes
segments.summary: A Simon Fraser University study sank a pig carcass near the Sailors Sea and found it reduced to bones in days, possibly due to high oxygen levels. A King County medical examiner study showed hands and feet detach at joints first. Athletic shoes with air-filled soles can float and protect a foot from scavengers.

segments.title: Frequency illusion and whether Vancouver is unusual
segments.summary: The hosts consider whether the cluster is real or a product of the frequency illusion, a cognitive bias tied to Arnold Zwicky and the bottom-line Huff phenomenon. They cite a NamUs search showing few disarticulated feet elsewhere in the US, suggesting Vancouver may be unusual.

segments.title: Internet Roundup listener story and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener describes a bumpy Delta flight into Austin during a thunderstorm, diverted to Houston, and says the show helped keep calm. The hosts then give contact details and sign off.
